verses.1:1: The elder, to Gaius the beloved, whom I love in truth.
verses.1:2: Beloved, above all things I pray that you may prosper and be in good health, even as your soul prospers.
verses.1:3: For I rejoiced exceedingly when brethren came and bore witness to your truth, even as you walk in truth.
verses.1:4: I have no greater joy than this: to hear that my own children walk in the truth.
verses.1:5: Beloved, you act faithfully in whatever you perform for the brethren, even though they are strangers,
verses.1:6: who have borne witness to your love before the church. You will do well to send them onward in a manner worthy of God.
verses.1:7: For on behalf of the Name they went forth, taking nothing from the Gentiles.
verses.1:8: We therefore ought to support such men, that we may become fellow workers for the truth.
verses.1:9: I wrote something to the church, but Diotrephes, who loves to be first among them, does not receive us.
verses.1:10: For this reason, if I come, I will bring to remembrance his deeds which he does, disparaging us with wicked words; and not content with these things, he himself does not receive the brethren, and he hinders those who desire to do so and casts them out of the church.
verses.1:11: Beloved, do not imitate that which is evil, but that which is good. He who does good is of God; he who does evil has not seen God.
verses.1:12: Demetrius has received a good witness from all, and from the truth itself; moreover, we also bear witness, and you know that our witness is true.
verses.1:13: I had many things to write to you, but I do not desire to write to you with ink and pen;
verses.1:14: rather, I hope to see you soon, and we shall speak face to face.
verses.1:15: Peace be to you. The friends greet you. Greet each of the friends by name.

notes.1:2: The Greek phrase peri panton ("above all things") is a common epistolary formula that can alternatively mean "in all respects," modifying "prosper and be in good health."
notes.1:5: Translates the critical Greek reading kai touto xenous ("and that though they are strangers"), emphasizing Gaius's faithful hospitality toward traveling brethren he did not personally know.
notes.1:7: The critical Greek text reads simply tou onomatos ("the Name"), an absolute reference to Christ (compare Acts 5:41), without the possessive pronoun "His" found in some later manuscripts.
notes.1:9: The critical Greek text includes ti ("something"), referring to an earlier brief letter sent by the elder to the church.
notes.1:14: The Greek idiom stoma pros stoma is literally "mouth to mouth," denoting direct personal conversation, rendered here as "face to face."
